AGENDA
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  VIA TELECONFERENCE ONLY
 Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and AT&T U-
 verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
 glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
 using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu. Meetings are also
 archived on the City Website for viewing anytime at glendaleca.gov/agendas. Call (818) 548-4013 for
 program schedules. DVDs of the proceedings are available for purchase in the City Clerk's Office.
 If you have any question about matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact the
 Management Services Department at (818) 548-4844, during regular business hours.
  PLEASE TURN OFF CELLULAR PHONES WHILE INSIDE THE MEETING LOCATION
 In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, auxiliary hearing aids, sign
 language translation, and Braille transcripts are available upon request. Assisted listening devices
 are available same-day upon request. At least 48 hours (or two business days) notice is required for
 requests regarding sign language translation and Braille transcription services. All documents related
 to open session items on this agenda that are received less than 72 hours prior to this meeting, and
 are public records, will be available for review in the Office of the City Clerk, 613 E. Broadway, RM
 110, Glendale, CA 91206.
 Translation services are provided for meetings through the use of bilingual staff for speakers who
 wish to utilize the service as available. Speakers should state their request by contacting the City
 Clerk’s office at (818) 548-2090, at least 24 hours prior to the scheduled meeting. Please specify
 the language for which you require translation. The exclusive use of City provided interpreters is not
 required and persons are welcome to use their own interpreter or speak in their native language.
  NOVEMBER 1, 2021 AT 6:30 PM

To help slow the transmission of COVID-19, and protect the health and safety of the community, City
Council, as well as Board & Commission meetings, will continue to be closed to the public for in-person
attendance.
The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes to practice social
distancing. Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and
AT&T U-verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu.
For public comments and questions during the meeting, call (818) 937-8100. Public comments on a
specific agenda item will be taken when that agenda item is discussed.

ROLL CALL
 1. REGULAR BUSINESS AGENDA
  a. Report of Recorder, re: Posting of Agenda. The Agenda for the November 1, 2021
  Blue Ribbon Pension Review Committee was Posted on October 29, 2021, on the
  Bulletin Board Outside City Hall.

3. MINUTES
  a. Approval of the minutes of the Regular Meeting on October 18, 2021.
4. BUSINESS ITEMS
  a. Presentation from Mary Beth Redding on Glendale’s Miscellaneous and Safety Plans
5. REPORTS - INFORMATION ONLY

CITY OF GLENDALE
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  REGULAR MEETING MINUTES

  November 1, 2021

ROLL CALL
Meeting starts at: 6:42pm

Present: Amirian, Manning, Finch, Masias, Molano, Palos, Holtzman, Bain, Wenz,
Kedikian, Wolfson, Michals

Absent: Knights, Nelson, Zakarian

Staff: Golanian, Doyle, Takhtalian, Garcia, Flynn, Hayrapetian, Hovsepian

1. REGULAR BUSINESS AGENDA
  a. Report of Recorder, re: Posting of Agenda. Ms. Hayrapetian announces that
  the agenda for the November 1, 2021 Blue Ribbon Pension Review
  Committee was Posted on October 29, 2021, on the Bulletin Board Outside
  City Hall.

2. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS
  None

  Wolfson suggests that Committee members have the option to make comments
  on each agenda item and notes that Committee members have not had enough
  time to raise questions in the past. She also notes that she does not think the
  Committee is on track to reach the Committee’s stated goal by the time January
  is over.
3. MINUTES
  a. Approval of the minutes of the Regular Meeting on October 18, 2021.

  Molano notes an inaccuracy in the minutes on page 6. Molano clarifies that the
  relevant issue is that congress may increase or do away with the limit on the
  level at which one gets taxed for social security, which is tied to the cap on
  pensionable compensation for PEPRA employees. If congress increases the
  former, it may increase the City’s pension obligation by raising the cap on
  pensionable compensation for PEPRA employees.

  Holtzman responds that the minutes will be amended to reflect that change.

  Wolfson notes that the minutes list Bain as present and as absent. Holtzman
responds that the minutes will be revised to reflect that Bain was absent.

  1
   Kedikian motions to accept the minutes as amended
  Amirian seconds

  Aye: Amirian, Kedikian, Manning, Masias, Michals, Molano, Wolfson, Finch,
Wenz, Palos
  No: none
  Abstain: Bain

  Motion passes.

4.BUSINESS ITEMS
  a. Presentation from Mary Beth Redding on Glendale’s Miscellaneous and Safety
  Plans

  Holtzman notes that before Mary Beth Redding presents, Garcia will present on
  the Brown Act

  Garcia screen shares a PowerPoint presentation on the Brown Act and reviews
  the following:
  • Purpose of Brown Act
  • General requirements
  • Legislative bodies covered by the Brown Act
  • Exceptions to what constitutes a meeting under the Brown Act
  • Serial meetings
  • Social media platforms (AB 992)
  • Public Access and Participation

  Molano asks about the City Council’s closed session meetings with employee
  representatives, and asks about how the public can challenge those closed
  sessions to open them up for the public.

  Garcia notes that there are legal issues regarding the meet and confer
  obligations that the City has with employee representatives and policy challenges
  regarding open negotiations.

  Wolfson thanks Garcia for the presentation and notes that she has some articles
  regarding the Brown Act that she will pass to Holtzman to pass to the rest of the
  Committee.

  Public Comment from Mike Mohill. Mike Mohill claims that City employees who
  are union members should not be part of the Committee. He claims that the goal
  of this group should be to terminate CalPERS, that all City employees should be

  2
 terminated and then rehired, and that the City needs to secure a pension bond to
pay off CalPERS and start from zero.

Holtzman introduces Mary Beth Redding.

Redding begins her presentation with a discussion of background info regarding
CalPERS.

Molano asks whether CalPERS provides the calculated liability to the City.
Redding notes that small agencies have to do some of the calculations
themselves.

Molano asks if the Cities receive the liability as bulk amount.
Redding answers yes.

Molano asks if the Committee can acquire details on the cost of beneifts for each
employee to arrive at the bulk number?
Redding answers no.

Molano asks when the City approved Management Association MOU last week,
why didn’t the City have the total pension liability in the MOU? Is that information
available on CalPERS website? When City approves the MOU it may have
significant impact on the total pension obligation. Is that info accessible to the
City Council before it approves the MOU?

Redding notes that the City could ask for that information, but there will be a
significant time delay before CalPERS could provide it.

Wolfson mentions that she is a CalPERS annuitant and participated in the
election of Board Members. She asks about what would it take for the Board to
be altered so that it would be composed of representatives who are members of
CalPERS system.

Holtzman responds that it would require a change to state law.

Amirian asks about the scope of questions permitted during the presentation and
requests that questions stay focused on the content in the slides.

Kedikian expresses agreement with Amirian’s request.

Redding continues her presentation. She notes that Glendale employees do not
get social security.

  3
 Kedikian asks about CalPERS’ active employee benefits. How much does
Glendale pay for employees who worked in another city before coming to
Glendale, but then retire from Glendale?

Redding answers that Glendale would be responsible for just a small bit of the
pension. The other City would be responsible for all the years at the other agency
plus their rate for the time in Glendale.

Wolfson notes that Social Security is also a defined benefit and that PERS
members might also qualify for social security if they work in private sector after
leaving Glendale.

Redding continues her presentation regarding what explains unfunded liabilities.

Molano asks about how CalPERS evaluates its assets given that it isn’t selling
them. He notes that when he sells stocks and recognizes gains on his
investments, he is taxed, but if he doesn’t sell them, then he doesn’t pay any
taxes on them.

Redding responds that their evaluation of assets follows the accounting rules: if
it’s a publicly traded security it’s the fair market value on the day of valuation.
She adds that the fund itself pays taxes

Molano comments that if the City lowers the age of retirement form 55 to 50, then
another chunk of liability is added, and expected life has grown too, so it creates
a big increase to liability that was not taken into account when the City adopted
the new benefits.

Kedikian asks: what’s an ideal ratio of active to retired employees, specifically in
Glendale?

Redding responds that there’s really no ideal ratio, but the ratio will continue to
grow. The only thing one can do is plan for it.

Holtzman notes that with really old cities, the ratios are even greater.

Redding notes that even in LA area there are higher ratios.

Wolfson asks about the composition of the CalPERS investment portfolio and
what they’re allowed to invest in.

Redding responds that the Board sets investment policy typically every 4 years
(the last being set in 2018).

  4
 Wolfson asks about the ratio of bonds vs. stocks.

Redding responds that they have a lot of specialty areas and the best thing to do
is look at their website.

Holtzman notes that CalPERS has been looking at venture capital and private
investment.

Wolfson comments that in the MOU with GMA the City will be paying part of the
employee share.

Takhtalian responds that this is not accurate: the employer does not pay any of
the employee share, the employee has to pay the full 8% the employee has to
also pay some of the employer share.

Masias asks: what % of CalPERS assets are needed to cover benefits for
retirees?

Redding notes that it’s not really calculated that way. For any given retiree, their
benefit has been funded as they worked their service. The City spends a little
each year and when an employee retires it’s all paid for. The amount CalPERS
receives in contributions is roughly equivalent to what they pay out in benefits.

Redding continues her presentation regarding risk mitigation and the differences
between miscellaneous and safety employees.

Molano asks whether CalPERS take recessions, earthquakes, etc. into their risk
calculation so that it can get a more realistic picture of economy?

Redding believes that they do.

Kedikian asks about the impact of inflation on the graph regarding the funded
status for miscellaneous.

Redding answers that they used 2.75% inflation assumption.

Redding continues her presentation with discussion of contribution projections for
miscellaneous. She notes that it is projected that by 2040 the unfunded liability
will be largely paid off due to phasing out of Classic employees and because the
City has paid large sums in the past.

Molano asks about CalPERS assumptions with regard to pay increases: if City
created an additional step, would it impact the City’s total obligation significantly?

  5
 Redding answers that what the CalPERS plan actually costs is equivalent to
what benefits are actually paid to a retiree, i.e. what pay really is when they
retire, which may, but also may not, depend on how many salary steps. Over a
person’s lifetime there’s a lot of competitive analysis to make sure things are
staying reasonably close in the market place. Actuaries use historic data on YOY
raises for people of certain ages and years of service. However, they don’t look
at MOUs, so MOUs don’t have a big impact on CalPERS’ assumptions.

Wolfson asks about how Redding knows that the UAL won’t continue to grow
dramatically in the way that it has since 2016.

Redding responds that starting in 2016, CalPERS recognized that things weren’t
going well and needed to make some changes. Some of the changes were very
radical and costly. All of them were phased in over a number of years. They
started the changes in 2016, but they won’t be fully phased in until 24/25. In
2016, the cost changes are starting to be phased in, and we’re now almost to the
end of that phase. Once we’re done with the phasing in, that’s when Redding
thinks the costs will start to come down.

Holtzman notes that they are talking about miscellaneous, not safety.

Bain asks: in reference to assumed salary increases, are those standard rate?

Redding responds that, for projections, they take all of the people in any one
pension plan and group them by everyone with the same number of years of
service and age, and then look at raises received on average every year. Every
single year they will then collect the actual numbers and do a true-up and look at
what people actually made in that year.

Amirian comments that during Takhtalian’s presentation in the 10/4/21 meeting,
he saw that the City had a choice between 3 amortization schedules. Amirian
asks whether the City Council had an option to choose between 3 different
schedule? Can the City choose different schedules for paying off the UAL?

Redding answers that the City has some options to pay faster, but cannot choose
to pay off more slowly. She notes that paying faster is economically a good
decision.

Amirian asks whether the projection models incorporate those different schedule
options?

Flynn notes that the City has made additional payments toward the UAL, and that
when the City does that, the City works with CalPERS to determine which

  6
 amortization basis is most beneficial and to which basis it wants to apply its
payment.

Redding continues her presentation with a discussion of Safety.

Holtzman notes that Glendale’s unfunded status is about the same for other
comparable cities, but its rates are quite different.

Redding adds that high rates can mean various things, e.g. contracting out
services reduces payroll and increases the rate.

Molano notes that he thinks it’s really important point to try and gauge what the
actual costs are for cities that have contracted out police and fire. He asks if
there is a way to obtain the actual cost, to see if it’s a viable option for Glendale.

Redding responds that she does not know much of the specifics. For example,
La Canada pays out a bill for their contracted police and fire, but it’s not clear
how much of that bill would be for pension. She adds that the negotiated rate
might also be set from years ago. She also notes that the Safety pension plan for
LA County will have a cost curve similar to the contribution projections she sees
for Glendale: a piece of the cost for contracted police and fire dedicated to
pension is probably dealing with the same increases you might just not know it.
Contracting out makes it hard to compare the numbers between agencies.

Redding continues her presentation with a discussion of withdrawing from
CalPERS.

Kedikian asks about the give and take, exposure, and risk associated with
leaving CalPERS.

Redding notes that when CalPERS says if they don’t earn 7%, then they can
come back and ask fore more in the future, but when they ask for 1.75% they’re
saying it’s their one and only shot.

Holtzman adds that he went against CalPERS on the issue of withdrawal a little
bit, but didn’t end up litigating. He comments that any actuary would think the
number is low because they are assuming all the risk that nothing will change in
future. Holtzman notes that it’s important to remember that pension plans have
very broad discretion to set rates in their fiduciary interest.

Molano asks: if an employee is terminated, say after 20 or 25 YOS, does the City
have to pay CalPERS any additional amount for unfunded portion, or does the
employee simply leave?

  7
   Redding responds that that person does have a pension: they worked for 25
  years, so they will get pension when they retire, and the City is responsible for
  making sure there’s enough money for that employee when they retire. At this
  point there’s UAL, and likely some of it applies to that individual, so they would
  likely still be paying up until that point.

  Holtzman notes that part of the issue is that UAL isn’t indexed to particular
  people, so it’s hard to see to whom the UAL is owed. There’s a legally obligation
  to retirees to pay their pensions, but UAL doesn’t have a real home.

  Molano asks to clarify for members of public that if CalPERS loses money on its
  investments, the taxpayer is still on the hook for that shortage.

  Redding responds that this is correct.

  Wolfson comments that the Committee keeps getting into a discussion about
  completely leaving CalPERS, but she does not know if anyone on the Committee
  has actually suggested doing that. She notes that there are a lot of options in the
  middle and that she thinks this is where the Committee needs to put its efforts.

  Holtzman notes that it is 9pm and suggests that we should stop for now and
  bring Redding back for further questions and discussion next time.

  Wolfson thanks the presenter.

  Public comment from Mike Mohill: Mohill expresses the view that the City needs
  to leave CalPERS.

  Kedikian asks about how to get items for agenda onto next meeting.

  Holtzman asks Kedikian or anyone else to contact him about agenda items

  Molano requests that at the next meeting Flynn explain how UAL is booked and
  whether it shows up in various department budget items.

5. REPORTS
  None.
6. REQUESTS FOR ITEMS ON FUTURE AGENDAS
  None.
7. ADJOURNMENT
  Kedikian moves to adjourn
  Seconded by Molano
  Meeting adjourns at 9:12pm
